title: Validating Graph Neural Network Feature Attribution Through Local Perturbations: A Study on CoMoFeNiCu Decomposition Enthalpy
authors: Miguel Tenorio, James Chapman
abstract: Graph neural networks (GNNs) show promise for predicting materials properties, but interpretability remains a challenge, particularly understanding whether attributed feature importance reflects physical reality or statistical artifacts. Here, we present a methods validation study that deliberately overfits a physics-aware GNN ensemble to probe the robustness of feature-ranking approaches. Using the CoMoFeNiCu high-entropy alloy system with three stoichiometries, we train GNNs to predict decomposition enthalpies from DFT-calculated structures while explicitly constraining output weights to encode feature importance. By design, our dataset is limited (approximately 900 binary and 4,500 ternary decomposition pathways) to control compositional complexity and enable precise interrogation of local chemistry effects. We validate that feature rankings capture meaningful local-environment information through a series of atomic swap perturbations: perturbing individual atomic sites and re-ranking features reveals spatial decay consistent with the GNN's interaction cutoff, confirming that weights encode neighbor-shell effects rather than global stoichiometric artifacts alone. Results demonstrate that feature attribution methods can remain physically interpretable even under overfitting, provided validation is rigorous. This work establishes a foundation for trustworthy interpretability in materials GNNs and sets the stage for scaling to multiple chemistries and testing generalization across compositional spaces.

infographic.key_insight: Local atomic-swap tests indicate that GNN feature rankings capture physically meaningful neighbor-shell effects, even under deliberate overfitting.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Perturbation-based validation can help engineers assess whether materials-model explanations reflect local chemistry rather than compositional artifacts.
method: Train a deliberately overfit, physics-aware GNN ensemble on DFT-derived CoMoFeNiCu decomposition enthalpies.
Constrain output weights to encode feature importance.
Swap individual atomic sites and re-rank features to probe spatial sensitivity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across three stoichiometries and approximately 900 binary and 4,500 ternary decomposition pathways, perturbation effects decayed spatially in a manner consistent with the GNN interaction cutoff.
infographic.watch_item: This controlled validation does not establish predictive generalization to unseen compositions or other alloy chemistries.
infographic.paper_title: Validating Graph Neural Network Feature Attribution Through Local Perturbations: A Study on CoMoFeNiCu Decomposition Enthalpy

title: Materials research with a general-purpose agent
authors: Paulo R. Pires, Théo Cavignac, Tiago F. T. Cerqueira, Hai-Chen Wang, Silvana Botti, Miguel A. L. Marques
abstract: Over the last decade we have built Alexandria, an open database of about 15 million density-functional calculations of crystals. It includes PBE, PBEsol, SCAN and TB-mBJ results, structures relaxed at pressures up to 150 GPa, dielectric tensors and about 145,000 electron-phonon calculations, together with more than 400 million structures relaxed with machine-learned potentials. On these data we trained a generative model for crystal structures, a universal interatomic potential and graph neural networks for more than ten properties, from band gaps to superconducting critical temperatures. From the convex hull we computed a reaction graph of the 17.4 billion reactions between its 193,416 stable compounds. Here we give all of this to a general-purpose language-model agent. Working unattended, the agent screens the database for a solar absorber, drops a candidate whose synthesis releases too little energy, and writes a synthesis plan with precursors, crucible and atmosphere. Asked about the well-studied Ba-Zr-S system, it finds an unreported sulfide and designs the experiment that would confirm or rule it out. Asked for an air-stable alternative, it designs one and tests it against new structures from the generative model. With web search alone, the same agent proposes what the literature already discusses. Put together, the data, the models and the reaction graph let a general agent do what none of them does alone: go from a question in plain words to an experiment that a laboratory can run and test.

infographic.key_insight: A general-purpose language-model agent combined with materials databases, predictive models and a reaction graph can turn plain-language questions into experimentally testable synthesis plans.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could streamline materials screening and synthesis planning by linking predicted properties, phase stability and practical laboratory choices.
method: Connect the agent to Alexandria’s crystal calculations and trained materials models.
Use a reaction graph to assess candidate compounds and synthesis energetics.
Generate synthesis plans and challenge proposed materials with newly generated structures.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports about 15 million DFT calculations and a 17.4-billion-reaction graph, with unattended case studies producing synthesis plans and an unreported sulfide candidate; web search alone returned literature-discussed options.
infographic.watch_item: The proposed materials and synthesis plans still require laboratory validation; the abstract reports no experimental confirmation.
infographic.paper_title: Materials research with a general-purpose agent

title: Crystal Structure Prediction from Search to Learning: A 30-Year Expedition
authors: Jianjun Hu, Ying Feng
abstract: Crystal structure prediction (CSP) determines periodic atomic or molecular arrangements from chemical composition and physical conditions. Over three decades, CSP has evolved from chemical construction and global energy optimization to hybrid approaches combining symmetry, learned potentials, adaptive search, and deep generative models. This survey reviews method, software, review, and benchmark records from 1996 to October 2026, covering inorganic and molecular crystals, including formula-conditioned diffusion, flow, and autoregressive models that preserve composition. We classify methods by candidate construction and exploration: template and discrete construction, random search, evolutionary search, swarm and differential evolution, energy-landscape exploration, adaptive machine-learning-guided search, and learned generation. We distinguish representation, relaxation, ranking, and physical qualification. Benchmarks reveal no universally dominant approach. In a 46-target leaderboard snapshot, the best-performing template method achieves higher top-1 recovery than leading generative models, but paired tests show no statistically significant differences from several generative competitors. We also audit predictions for 68 experimentally examined materials, including 52 with structures confirmed by diffraction or microscopy. Predictions for 23 of the 68 preceded experiment, mostly through first-principles global search. Within the reviewed evidence, we find no independently confirmed discovery in which a deep generative model predicted the structure before experiment. We conclude with the principal limitations of current CSP algorithms and priorities for future research.

infographic.key_insight: Across three decades, crystal structure prediction has expanded from global search to learned generation, but no approach consistently dominates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Reliable materials discovery requires evaluating candidate generation separately from structural relaxation, ranking, and physical qualification.
method: Survey CSP methods, software, reviews, and benchmarks from 1996 to October 2026.
Classify approaches by candidate construction and exploration, from template search to deep generative models.
Compare benchmark recovery and audit experimentally examined predictions.
infographic.evidence_signal: A 46-target leaderboard favors a template method on top-1 recovery without significant paired differences from several generative competitors; among 68 experimentally examined materials, 52 had confirmed structures and 23 predictions preceded experiment.
infographic.watch_item: Within the reviewed evidence, no independently confirmed discovery involved a deep generative model predicting the structure before experiment.
infographic.paper_title: Crystal Structure Prediction from Search to Learning: A 30-Year Expedition

title: A Machine-learning-aided Workflow for Sampling Small Polaron Dynamics in Energy Materials
authors: Tavinder Singh, Harald Oberhofer
abstract: One of the defining characteristics of most energy materials, used as e.g.~battery electrodes, photovoltaics, or photocatalysts, is their ability conduct charges such as electrons and holes. The exact mechanism of this conductivity depends on the material, but is often dominated by the existence of mobile small polarons, i.e.~electrons or holes strongly localised through the polarisation of their environment. Computationally, small polarons can be treated with reasonably accuracy through the use of self-interaction corrected or hybrid density functional theory (DFT) together with local geometry optimisation. Similar approaches can be employed to determine the energy barriers to movement of the polarons through hopping. Unfortunately, realistic energy materials tend have very large numbers of symmetry inequivalent polaronic configurations and correspondingly large numbers of hopping barriers, making them hard to tackle explicitly. In this work we therefore extend the computational reach of DFT calculations with machine-learned (ML) surrogate models, which then feed into a kinetic model to quantitatively estimate the conductivity of a battery anode material (Li$_4$Ti$_5$O$_12$ or LTO) at realistic, defected conditions. We calculate the conductivity at room temperature to be 6.7 $\times$ 10$^{-3}$ S/cm which lies well in the experimental range. To this end, we only needed a total of 154 polaron barrier calculations, out of 3649 symmetry inequivalent ones, achieving an over 20-fold increase of computational efficiency. Overall, our work demonstrates how DFT-trained ML surrogates can be used to quantitatively and efficiently sample the dynamics of small polarons in energy materials.

infographic.key_insight: DFT-trained machine-learning surrogates enable efficient sampling of small-polaron hopping and quantitative conductivity prediction in defected Li₄Ti₅O₁₂ (LTO).
infographic.engineering_relevance: The workflow reduces the computational cost of modeling charge transport in a battery anode material under realistic defect conditions.
method: Calculate small-polaron configurations and hopping barriers using DFT.
Train ML surrogates to estimate barriers across symmetry-inequivalent hopping pathways.
Feed surrogate predictions into a kinetic model to estimate conductivity.
infographic.evidence_signal: Using 154 barrier calculations out of 3,649 symmetry-inequivalent cases, the workflow achieved over 20-fold computational efficiency and predicted room-temperature conductivity of 6.7 × 10⁻³ S/cm, within the experimental range.
infographic.watch_item: Validation beyond LTO remains necessary; accuracy may depend on whether DFT training data cover the relevant defect environments and hopping pathways.
infographic.paper_title: A Machine-learning-aided Workflow for Sampling Small Polaron Dynamics in Energy Materials

title: CGTransformer: A Topology-Aware Autoregressive Framework for Crystal Generation and Inverse Design
authors: Zhennan Zhang, Shaobo Yu, Haoting Zhang, Yu Han, Zhiyue Guo, Junjie Wang
abstract: Autoregressive language models offer a unified route to crystal generation and inverse design, but their performance depends on how periodic structures are serialized. Symmetry equivalent and closely related crystals can receive different atomic orders under coordinate-based serialization, introducing variability unrelated to their structural connectivity. Here, we present CGTransformer (Crystal Graph Transformer), an autoregressive generative framework that addresses this challenge via a graph-embedded sorting strategy. Using quotientgraph topology and barycentric embeddings, Element Symmetry Graph (ESG) converts periodic crystal networks into topology-guided one-dimensional sequences that retain key local and symmetry-related structural information. CGTransformer achieves high generation validity and the highest single shot crystal structure prediction (CSP) match rate among the compared MP-20 baselines (63.24%), while same backbone comparisons show improved structure recovery over coordinate-based ordering. Furthermore, we demonstrate property-conditioned inverse design for wide-bandgap semiconductors, where ESG achieves a much higher stable, unique and novel (S.U.N.) rate and stronger target-property alignment than the coordinate-based baseline. These results establish topology-guided sequence construction as an effective route to improving crystal generation and property-directed design at fixed model capacity.

infographic.key_insight: CGTransformer improves autoregressive crystal generation by ordering atoms using crystal topology rather than coordinates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Topology-guided sequences improve structure recovery at fixed model capacity and support property-targeted design of wide-bandgap semiconductors.
method: Represent periodic crystal connectivity with quotient graphs.
Use Element Symmetry Graph (ESG) sorting and barycentric embeddings to construct topology-guided sequences.
Train an autoregressive transformer for crystal generation and property-conditioned inverse design.
infographic.evidence_signal: On MP-20, CGTransformer achieves a 63.24% single-shot crystal structure prediction match rate—the highest among compared baselines—and ESG improves structure recovery and stable, unique, novel generation over coordinate-based ordering.
infographic.watch_item: Performance beyond the reported benchmark and semiconductor targets remains to be established; implementation also requires reliable graph construction and barycentric embedding.
infographic.paper_title: CGTransformer: A Topology-Aware Autoregressive Framework for Crystal Generation and Inverse Design

title: Enrichment-Oriented Virtual Screening of Perovskite Solar Cells through Reinforcement Learning
authors: Yezeyuan Zheng, Ziyang Hu, Maojun Sun. Ruijian Han, Jian Huang, Guanhua Chen, Jie Liu
abstract: Experimental optimization of perovskite solar cells is constrained by combinatorial diversity in absorber compositions, device layers, and processing, which makes virtual screening attractive for prioritizing recipes before fabrication. We develop a surrogate-guided reinforcement-learning framework that casts recipe generation as virtual screening, enriching candidate shortlists near high-performing experimental neighbors. A frozen Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (TabPFN) guides recipe generation, while a reference pool of 890 measured devices enables neighborhood-based assessment. Five-fold evaluation on 1,846 devices shows top-ten selection raises mean power conversion efficiency (PCE) from 19.68\% to 23.74\%. Three learned policies are compared with six baselines under 3,000 surrogate evaluations per run. In top-100 shortlists, Proximal policy optimization (PPO) and recurrent PPO (RPPO) achieve neighborhood-supported hit rates of 23\% and 24\% (7.9- and 8.3-fold Pure Random's 2.9\%), versus 10\% (3.4-fold) for the baselines with the highest supported hit rate (L-SHADE and Ax BO, tied) at $K = 100$. Gains coexist with weak-support fractions. Of 9,000 recipes, 65.4\% match a composition family at similarity 0.80, falling to 11.7\% at 0.90. Results support enrichment-oriented prioritization but not experimental performance, seed robustness, or matched-budget advantage.

infographic.key_insight: Surrogate-guided reinforcement learning enriched perovskite recipe shortlists near high-performing measured devices, without establishing experimental performance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could help prioritize perovskite solar-cell recipes for fabrication across a large composition, device-layer, and processing space.
method: Use a frozen Tabular Prior-data Fitted Network (TabPFN) to guide recipe generation.
Compare three learned policies with six baselines using 3,000 surrogate evaluations per run.
Assess candidate support through neighborhoods in a reference pool of 890 measured devices.
infographic.evidence_signal: In top-100 shortlists, PPO and recurrent PPO achieved neighborhood-supported hit rates of 23% and 24%, versus 2.9% for Pure Random and 10% for the strongest baselines on this metric.
infographic.watch_item: Only 11.7% of 9,000 generated recipes matched a composition family at similarity 0.90; experimental performance, seed robustness, and matched-budget advantage remain unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Enrichment-Oriented Virtual Screening of Perovskite Solar Cells through Reinforcement Learning

title: Brute-force molecular dynamics simulation of aging in amorphous Ge$_2$Sb$_2$Te$_5$
authors: Elisa Petroni, Dario Baratella, Omar Abou El Kheir, Andrea Redaelli, Marco Bernasconi
abstract: Chalcogenide alloys such as the prototypical Ge$_2$Sb$_2$Te$_5$ compound are used in phase change electronic memories due to their ability to undergo a fast and reversible transition between the amorphous and crystalline phases upon heating. The amorphous phase is subject to aging that leads to an increase in the electrical resistance, which is detrimental to the operation of the devices. Using a machine learning interatomic potential, we have investigated the structural relaxations responsible for aging in amorphous Ge$_2$Sb$_2$Te$_5$ in molecular dynamics simulations at temperatures slightly below the glass transition. The aging simulation, lasting about 100 ns, follows an equilibration of 24 ns at 400 K. During aging we observed an enhancement of the Peierls distortion in axial bonds which is a typical feature of these alloys that we relate to the widening of the electronic band gap computed within Density Functional Theory in smaller aged amorphous models. We also observed a marked reduction of the atomic mobility with an increase of the bond lifetimes during aging. However, we do not see a reduction in homopolar bonds, which are expected to be absent in the ideal aged glass and which should be removed on a much longer time scale.

infographic.key_insight: Machine-learning-driven molecular dynamics links aging in amorphous Ge₂Sb₂Te₅ to enhanced axial-bond Peierls distortion, a wider electronic band gap, and reduced atomic mobility.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These structural insights help explain resistance drift that degrades the reliability of phase-change memory devices.
method: Simulate amorphous Ge₂Sb₂Te₅ using a machine-learning interatomic potential.
Follow 24 ns of equilibration at 400 K with approximately 100 ns of aging.
Compute electronic band gaps in smaller aged amorphous models using density functional theory.
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulations show stronger Peierls distortion and longer bond lifetimes during aging, while DFT calculations associate aging with band-gap widening.
infographic.watch_item: Homopolar bonds did not decrease over the simulated interval, leaving longer-timescale structural relaxation unresolved.
infographic.paper_title: Brute-force molecular dynamics simulation of aging in amorphous Ge$_2$Sb$_2$Te$_5$

title: SiC-BN composites with extreme thermal and environmental stability
authors: Abhijit Biswas, Eugenio Garcia-Granados, Saman Zare, Mozhdeh Mirakhory, JungHun Park, Shuvodeep De
abstract: Ceramic materials that maintain structural integrity and resist thermal-shock under extreme conditions are critical for many applications. Here we show that spark plasma sintered composites containing equal weight fractions of hexagonal silicon carbide (6H-SiC) and boron nitride (h-BN) exhibit exceptional stability under extreme high-temperature oxidizing conditions and unusually stable temperature-independent thermal conductivity across a broad temperature range. Under high-velocity oxygen-fuel torch exposure in air, it withstands prolonged heating and thermal-cycling at surface temperatures reaching >1500 °C, whereas pure 6H-SiC and h-BN rapidly fractures or erodes. Microstructural evaluation shows the formation of a multi-phase surface silica layer that further protects the material from oxidation. Finite-element analysis heat-flux map shows that intrinsic porosity mitigates thermal stress, while ReaxFF molecular dynamics simulations reveal thermally driven interfacial reconstruction and the formation of a Si-N/C-B-rich bonding network, enhancing the interfacial cohesion at elevated temperatures. This lightweight, easily machinable ceramic composite will be a promising structural material in extreme environment applications.

infographic.key_insight: An equal-weight 6H-SiC/h-BN composite withstands extreme oxidizing heat while maintaining unusually temperature-independent thermal conductivity.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This lightweight, machinable ceramic could enable structural components that resist thermal shock and oxidation in extreme environments.
method: Spark plasma sintering of equal-weight 6H-SiC and h-BN.
High-velocity oxygen-fuel torch testing and microstructural evaluation.
Finite-element heat-flux analysis and ReaxFF molecular dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The composite survived prolonged heating and thermal cycling at surface temperatures above 1500 °C, while pure 6H-SiC and h-BN rapidly fractured or eroded; microscopy identified a protective multiphase silica surface layer.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not quantify exposure duration, cycle count, or retained mechanical strength, limiting assessment of service lifetime.
infographic.paper_title: SiC-BN composites with extreme thermal and environmental stability

title: Quantum Material Generation via Coherent Hamiltonian Search
authors: Jiang Yuhan, Matthew Otten
abstract: Discovering new materials with targeted properties is a central goal of materials science, yet the space of candidates is vast. Data-driven generative models learn the distribution of known materials, but they extrapolate poorly, and a generated structure is not known to be stable. A material's properties follow from its Hamiltonian, and a quantum computer can calculate them from it. We introduce the quantum material generative algorithm (QMage), a coherent search, guided by the Hamiltonian, over crystalline configurations of atomic composition, unit cell structure, and atomic positions, for one whose calculated properties meet the targets to within a given error tolerance. The computation is a single coherent quantum circuit in which each configuration's Hamiltonian is block-encoded, its target eigenstate isolated and properties evaluated, and the satisfying configurations amplified by fixed-point search and measured. One framework covers many targets, from formation energy and band gaps to elasticity and conductivity. We design the algorithm for the mature fault-tolerant era and estimate its cost in logical qubits and Toffoli depth from a classically routine benchmark to targets where established methods are unreliable. The approach generates candidate materials from first principles, rather than generalizing from those known, and could enable materials discovery when the target properties are difficult to predict classically.

infographic.key_insight: QMage proposes a coherent quantum search for crystalline materials whose first-principles properties meet specified targets within an error tolerance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could support inverse design for formation energy, band gaps, elasticity, and conductivity without relying on extrapolation from known materials.
method: Search coherently over atomic compositions, unit cell structures, and atomic positions.
Block-encode each configuration’s Hamiltonian, isolate its target eigenstate, and evaluate properties.
Amplify configurations satisfying the targets using fixed-point search, then measure candidates.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports logical-qubit and Toffoli-depth cost estimates spanning a classically routine benchmark and targets where established methods are unreliable, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: QMage is designed for mature fault-tolerant quantum computers, so practical deployment depends on hardware capabilities and resource requirements not quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Quantum Material Generation via Coherent Hamiltonian Search

title: Graph diffusion transformer for interpretable generation and inverse design of disordered atomic structures
authors: Jiani Hu, Chenyan Wang, Yongkun Yang, Guanyu Hou, Jihaochen Zhang, Lei Liu
abstract: Atomic disorder offers a potent degree of freedom to tailor material properties, yet the resulting vast configuration space obscures structure-property relations and hinders rational inverse design. Here we introduce Graph Amorphous Diffusion Transformer (GaDiT), a generative model that combines dynamic periodic graphs, masked conditioning and an interval-weighted training-noise distribution. GaDiT generates high-quality disordered structures while accelerating sampling by two orders of magnitude compared with existing corrector-based approaches, as demonstrated across two-dimensional amorphous carbon and three-dimensional amorphous silicon and silica. Moreover, GaDiT supports conditional generation under single or combined structural features, physical properties and preparation conditions in a unified model, and enables inverse design that expands accessible structure-property ranges beyond the training distribution. To interpret these structures and the trained network, we propose a conditioned atomic response mapping analysis, revealing both the global structural descriptors and the local atomic environments that govern target properties. Overall, GaDiT establishes a general framework for interpretable generation, inverse design and structure-property discovery for disordered atomic structures.

infographic.key_insight: GaDiT generates disordered atomic structures and enables interpretable inverse design toward target properties, including beyond training-distribution ranges.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could accelerate exploration of amorphous materials by linking atomic disorder to desired properties and preparation conditions.
method: Combines dynamic periodic graphs with a diffusion transformer.
Uses masked conditioning and an interval-weighted training-noise distribution.
Applies conditioned atomic response mapping to identify influential structural descriptors and local environments.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 2D amorphous carbon and 3D amorphous silicon and silica, the abstract reports high-quality generation and sampling two orders of magnitude faster than existing corrector-based approaches.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish physical validation or generalization beyond the demonstrated material systems.
infographic.paper_title: Graph diffusion transformer for interpretable generation and inverse design of disordered atomic structures

title: Pressure dependent DFT study of mechanical, thermal, electronic, magnetic, and optical properties of EuCd2As2: a magnetic semimetal
authors: Salauddin Muhammad Anis, M. A. Afzal, R. S. Islam, S. H. Naqib
abstract: We present a comprehensive spin-polarized density functional theory (DFT) investigation of the pressure-dependent physical properties of EuCd2As2, a magnetically and topologically rich compound with potential applications in spintronics and optoelectronics technologies. We have investigated the structural, mechanical, thermophysical, acoustic, electronic, magnetic, and optical properties of this material at pressures of 0, 2, 4, 6, and 8 GPa. The calculated lattice parameters at zero pressure are in good agreement with experimental values. The mechanical stability of EuCd2As2 is maintained over the investigated pressure range. The elastic constants, bulk modulus, shear modulus, and Young's modulus are found to be tunable with applied pressure. The compound undergoes a brittle to ductile transition at higher pressures. The Debye temperature, melting temperature, and Grüneisen parameter are found to be strongly pressure-dependent. Phonon thermal conductivity has been evaluated. The electronic properties of EuCd2As2 were studied through band structure and density of states (DOS). The effect of pressure up to 8 GPa was investigated for the ferromagnetic (FM) phase. At 0 GPa, the calculated FM band structure exhibits no band gap at the Fermi level, which confirms the semimetallic nature of EuCd2As2. The net magnetic moment of 6.96 μ_B per unit cell was obtained for this compound indicating its potential for spintronics application. The optical properties, including the dielectric function, refractive index, absorption coefficient, optical conductivity, reflectivity, and loss function, are calculated. The calculated optical spectra indicate strong absorption in the visible and ultraviolet regions, suggesting that EuCd2As2 may have potential for optoelectronic applications.

infographic.key_insight: Spin-polarized DFT predicts that pressure tunes EuCd2As2’s mechanical and thermophysical properties while preserving mechanical stability from 0 to 8 GPa.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Its predicted magnetic moment and strong visible–ultraviolet absorption suggest potential for spintronic and optoelectronic materials engineering.
method: Spin-polarized DFT at 0, 2, 4, 6, and 8 GPa.
Structural, elastic, acoustic, and thermophysical calculations.
Ferromagnetic band structure, DOS, magnetic, and optical analysis.
infographic.evidence_signal: Zero-pressure lattice parameters agree with experiment; calculations predict a pressure-induced brittle-to-ductile transition, no Fermi-level band gap at 0 GPa, and a net moment of 6.96 μB per unit cell.
infographic.watch_item: Pressure-dependent predictions and device relevance require experimental validation; the reported electronic pressure study considers the ferromagnetic phase.
infographic.paper_title: Pressure dependent DFT study of mechanical, thermal, electronic, magnetic, and optical properties of EuCd2As2: a magnetic semimetal

title: Machine-learning charge density for electronic materials and devices simulation
authors: Qingyun Zhang, Yang Hu, Aixia Zhang, Zehua Sun, Jiawei Yan, Xiaohao Zhou
abstract: We present a machine-learning (ML) charge density model, DeltaChargeNet, integrated with the full-potential tight-binding muffin-tin orbital (FP-TB-MTO) method for electronic structure and quantum transport simulations of materials and devices. The ML model predicts electron density from atomic structures with low linear-scaling cost, while FP-TB-MTO provides an accurate tight-binding representation of the system Hamiltonian. To achieve high-fidelity ML density for complex devices with interfaces and disorder, we train an equivariant graph convolutional network to predict $Δρ$-the difference between DFT and atomic superposition densities-under a charge neutrality constraint required for inhomogeneous systems. A secondary ML residual charge model compensates for errors in the primary $Δρ$ model. The predicted density is then used within the full-relativistic FP-TB-MTO framework combined with the non-equilibrium Green's function method. We validate our method on bulk HgCdTe disordered alloys (including vacancy defects) and Au/HgCdTe/Au disordered devices. The maximum band energy error is below 10 meV for bulk HgCdTe. For devices, the charge neutrality constraint suppresses long-wavelength charge bias that would otherwise distort the electrostatic potential by 0.68-1.88 eV near the device center, while residual compensation corrects the remaining 0.16-0.46 eV potential mismatch, essential for reproducing the correct potential barrier profile. Together, these corrections reproduce the layer-resolved potential, including interface steps and bulk-like plateaus, within 0.1 eV of fully self-consistent DFT. Finally, we demonstrate quantum transport in a 11220-atom infrared detector. By combining first-principles accuracy with linear-scaling inference, DeltaChargeNet enables large-scale device simulations without the full DFT self-consistent field loop.

infographic.key_insight: DeltaChargeNet predicts charge density from atomic structures, enabling large-scale electronic and quantum transport simulations without the full DFT self-consistency loop.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach supports simulations of disordered semiconductor devices while preserving electrostatic barriers critical to transport predictions.
method: Train an equivariant graph network to predict density corrections relative to atomic superposition, enforcing charge neutrality.
Apply a secondary ML model to compensate for residual charge-density errors.
Use predicted densities with full-relativistic FP-TB-MTO and non-equilibrium Green’s functions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Tests on HgCdTe alloys and Au/HgCdTe/Au devices achieved maximum bulk band-energy errors below 10 meV and layer-resolved potentials within 0.1 eV of self-consistent DFT; transport was demonstrated for an 11,220-atom infrared detector.
infographic.watch_item: Transferability beyond the tested material systems remains unestablished, and both charge neutrality and residual compensation are important for accurate device potentials.
infographic.paper_title: Machine-learning charge density for electronic materials and devices simulation

title: New Closed-Form Approximations in Statistical Mechanics Obtained by Symbolic Regression
authors: Omkar Kunjir, Alina Popova, Rasul Abdusalamov, Mikhail Itskov
abstract: Obtaining accurate and analytically tractable closed-form expressions for complex physical systems remains a fundamental challenge in statistical mechanics. In this work, we investigate three approximation problems in polymer statistical mechanics using two complementary symbolic regression frameworks: Deep Symbolic Optimization (DSO), based on reinforcement learning, and PyOperon, based on genetic programming with nonlinear least-squares constant optimization. First, for the force-extension relationship of the Worm-Like Chain (WLC) model, DSO achieves a maximum relative error below 0.15%, while PyOperon reduces it to 0.05%, outperforming the Marko-Siggia formula (approximately 17%) and the Petrosyan approximation. Second, for the logarithmic factorial, ln(n!), both frameworks recover the dominant structure of Stirling's formula directly from analytical data. Using residual learning on a continued-fraction expansion of the Stirling remainder, PyOperon reduces the maximum relative error by a factor of 1.3 x 10^4 compared with the most accurate of nine classical approximations for n in [1, 30]. Third, for the non-Gaussian radial probability density of the Freely Jointed Chain (FJC) model, physics-informed residual learning improves the approximation by factors of 11.2 over Darabi et al. (2023) and 4.6 over the steepest-descent approximation. The discovered expressions remain analytically tractable across all three applications. These results demonstrate the complementary capabilities of DSO and PyOperon for discovering accurate closed-form approximations in statistical and continuum mechanics.

infographic.key_insight: Symbolic regression discovers analytically tractable approximations that substantially improve accuracy across three polymer statistical mechanics problems.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More accurate closed-form expressions could improve polymer constitutive models while preserving analytical tractability.
method: Use reinforcement-learning-based Deep Symbolic Optimization and genetic-programming-based PyOperon.
Fit expressions for WLC force–extension, ln(n!), and FJC radial probability density.
Apply residual learning, including physics-informed residuals for the FJC model.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported maximum relative errors for WLC are below 0.15% with DSO and 0.05% with PyOperon; approximation improvements reach 13,000-fold for ln(n!) on n ∈ [1, 30] and 11.2-fold over Darabi et al. for FJC density.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy outside the evaluated ranges and robustness when embedded in engineering simulations require further validation.
infographic.paper_title: New Closed-Form Approximations in Statistical Mechanics Obtained by Symbolic Regression

title: Diffusion Tree Sampling for Inference Time Adaptation of Crystal Generative Models
authors: Daniel T. Levy, Vineet Jain, Tara Akhound-Sadegh, Sékou-Oumar Kaba, Siamak Ravanbakhsh
abstract: Diffusion-based generative models have become strong priors over plausible crystal structures, but turning that prior into promising candidates requires steering toward several conflicting properties at once. Fine-tuning is expensive and produces a new model for every new objective, while differentiable guidance is not applicable to many real-world tasks. We instead adapt these generative models at inference time using Diffusion Tree Sampling (DTS), a Monte Carlo tree search procedure over the denoising trajectory. We make two technical contributions on top of DTS that are particularly relevant for AI-for-science applications. First, we show how to use existing property-conditional generative models (e.g., models fine-tuned for classifier-free guidance) as guided proposals inside DTS, without distorting the target distribution. Second, we extend DTS to multi-objective sampling, so that a single search produces samples spanning an entire Pareto front. We instantiate both adaptations on de novo crystal generation: improving the stability of crystals generated by different models, using pretrained conditional models to generate crystals belonging to rare space groups or with high bulk modulus, and generating crystals along a Pareto front of high dielectric constant and high bandgap materials. Across these tasks, DTS-based inference-time adaptation successfully improves model outputs without modifying the models themselves.

infographic.key_insight: Diffusion Tree Sampling steers crystal generative models at inference time toward desired properties and Pareto trade-offs without retraining.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Engineers can reuse pretrained crystal generators to explore candidates with improved stability or targeted mechanical, electronic, and dielectric properties.
method: Use Monte Carlo tree search over diffusion denoising trajectories.
Integrate property-conditional models as guided proposals without distorting the target distribution.
Extend sampling to cover a Pareto front of competing objectives in one search.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved crystal stability, generation targeting rare space groups or high bulk modulus, and Pareto-front sampling for high dielectric constant and high bandgap, but provides no numerical results.
infographic.watch_item: Practical utility depends on property-evaluation accuracy and tree-search cost, neither quantified in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Diffusion Tree Sampling for Inference Time Adaptation of Crystal Generative Models

title: Sample-efficient prediction of high-entropy alloy strength through outcome-aware robust sequential learning
authors: Ahmed Shoyeb Raihan, Md Habibor Rahman, Ashish Nimbarte, Imtiaz Ahmed
abstract: Accurate prediction of high-entropy alloy (HEA) strength can guide composition and processing decisions; however, obtaining tensile-test data for HEAs can be costly and experimentally demanding. This study proposes Robust Outcome-aware Sequential Experimentation for High-Entropy Alloys (ROSE-HEA), a sample-efficient framework for predicting ultimate tensile strength (UTS) from alloy composition and processing conditions. Its acquisition policy anticipates how possible UTS outcomes update predictions and the support for complementary Gaussian process (GP) descriptions. It then reassesses the worst-case expected predictive risk remaining across a reference domain to select informative candidates. A retrospective evaluation on 501 HEA records compares ROSE-HEA with expected-improvement (EI) and upper-confidence-bound (UCB) Bayesian optimization (BO), random GP sampling, and eight conventional regressors across 30 matched runs with shared initial observations and test conditions. Starting from 25 initial observations and acquiring 100 additional responses, ROSE-HEA achieves the lowest mean root-mean-square error (RMSE), at 152.84 MPa, and the highest mean R^2, at 0.7443. Mean RMSE is reduced by 6.16% and 6.37% relative to EI and UCB, respectively. The selected observations improve prediction across six regressor families and provide broader design-space coverage. ROSE-HEA also surpasses the strongest conventional regressor's mean predictive performance using 125 rather than 185 observations, corresponding to 32.4% fewer training observations. These findings demonstrate the potential of outcome-aware robust sequential learning to improve UTS prediction in HEAs under constrained training budgets.

infographic.key_insight: ROSE-HEA predicts high-entropy alloy strength more accurately with fewer training observations by selecting experiments based on possible outcomes and worst-case predictive risk.
infographic.engineering_relevance: More sample-efficient strength prediction could help engineers prioritize costly tensile tests when exploring alloy compositions and processing conditions.
method: Predict ultimate tensile strength from alloy composition and processing using complementary Gaussian process models.
Anticipate how candidate test outcomes would update predictions and support for each model.
Select candidates to reduce worst-case expected predictive risk across a reference design domain.
infographic.evidence_signal: In retrospective evaluation on 501 HEA records across 30 matched runs, ROSE-HEA achieved 152.84 MPa mean RMSE and 0.7443 mean R² with 125 observations, surpassing the strongest conventional regressor's mean predictive performance using 185 observations.
infographic.watch_item: Results are retrospective; prospective experimental validation is needed to establish performance on newly synthesized alloys.
infographic.paper_title: Sample-efficient prediction of high-entropy alloy strength through outcome-aware robust sequential learning

title: Competing Octahedral Tilting and $B$-Site Off-Centering Govern the Phase Diagram of CsGe$_{1-x}$Sn$_x$Br$_3$ Perovskite Alloys
authors: Apinya Ngoipala, Erik Fransson, Paul Erhart, Julia Wiktor
abstract: Lead-free halide perovskites based on Ge and Sn avoid the toxicity of Pb, but the two cations favor different structural distortions. The stereochemically active Ge $4s^2$ lone pair drives polar $B$-site off-centering, whereas the larger Sn$^{2+}$ cation favors octahedral tilting. Here, we map how these two instabilities compete across the full composition range of CsGe$_{1-x}$Sn$_x$Br$_3$ using large-scale molecular dynamics simulations with a charge-aware machine-learned interatomic potential trained on hybrid-functional data. At low temperature the alloy exhibits a morphotropic phase boundary between $x=0.60$ and $0.65$ that separates a ferroelectric monoclinic $Cc$ phase from a monoclinic $P2_1$ phase with mixed antipolar and polar off-centering, with both the tilt pattern and the off-centering order changing discontinuously. The composition-temperature phase diagram reproduces the known transition sequences and temperatures of both end members and reveals an intermediate tetragonal $I4/mcm$ phase near the boundary that has no counterpart in either parent compound. Above the transition temperatures the $B$ cations remain locally off-centered but orientationally disordered. The structural transition at the boundary causes a jump in the band gap at low temperature, whereas at $350$ K the gap decreases smoothly with Sn content. These results establish $B$-site mixing as a means to tune polar and rotational order in lead-free halide perovskites.

infographic.key_insight: Competing Ge-driven polar off-centering and Sn-favored octahedral tilting create a low-temperature phase boundary at 60–65% Sn in lead-free CsGe₁₋ₓSnₓBr₃.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Ge/Sn mixing offers a route to tune polar order, octahedral rotations, and band gaps in lead-free halide perovskites.
method: Train a charge-aware machine-learned interatomic potential on hybrid-functional data.
Run large-scale molecular dynamics across the full Ge/Sn composition range.
Map temperature-dependent phases, structural distortions, and band-gap trends.
infographic.evidence_signal: The simulated phase diagram reproduces reported transition sequences and temperatures for both end members and predicts an intermediate I4/mcm phase near the alloy boundary.
infographic.watch_item: The predicted alloy phase boundary and intermediate phase require experimental validation; agreement for the end members alone does not establish alloy accuracy.
infographic.paper_title: Competing Octahedral Tilting and $B$-Site Off-Centering Govern the Phase Diagram of CsGe$_{1-x}$Sn$_x$Br$_3$ Perovskite Alloys

title: Fine-tuned atomistic foundation model for accurate sodium-carbon chemistry in Na-ion batteries
authors: Andres Felipe Usuga, Ihor Radchenko, Yuxin Tang, Oleksandr I. Malyi
abstract: Atomistic foundation models have emerged as a promising route to DFT-level accuracy for materials simulation with complex chemical environments. However, their reliability across competing bonding regimes and, more importantly, how complex bonding affects predictions of material properties remain unclear. Among materials with competing bonding regimes, sodium storage in hard carbon poses a substantial challenge. Hard carbon features diverse local structural motifs, including defective and curved graphitic regions, amorphous regions, and closed/open pores. Motivated by its importance for Na-ion batteries, we systematically evaluate existing pretrained foundation models based on the MACE architecture across different local Na/C motifs. We find that the pretrained models fail to accurately capture Na-Na and Na-C interactions for metallic Na clusters on graphene. To recover a DFT-level energetic description, we employ targeted fine-tuning, showing that it can describe the energetic stability of local motifs and achieve sufficient transferability to unseen Na/C environments. With the developed fine-tuned model, we establish a correlation between closed-pore radius in hard carbon and plateau voltage, showing that the small pores contribute at larger voltages than large ones, suggesting thus how the developed fine-tuned foundation model can link atomistic information with materials design for complex bonding environments.

infographic.key_insight: Targeted fine-tuning of a MACE atomistic foundation model improves Na–C energetics and links smaller closed pores in hard carbon to higher sodium-storage plateau voltages.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model could guide hard-carbon pore design for Na-ion batteries by connecting local atomic structure with storage voltage.
method: Evaluate pretrained MACE models across diverse local Na/C motifs.
Fine-tune to recover DFT-level energetics for competing bonding environments.
Use the fine-tuned model to relate closed-pore radius to plateau voltage.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports pretrained-model failures for Na–Na and Na–C interactions in metallic Na clusters on graphene, followed by improved motif energetics and transferability to unseen Na/C environments after fine-tuning.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract provides no numerical error metrics or validation scope, so reliability across broader hard-carbon structures remains to be established.
infographic.paper_title: Fine-tuned atomistic foundation model for accurate sodium-carbon chemistry in Na-ion batteries

title: Verifiable pXRD: Hill-climbing pXRD structure determination with LLM agents
authors: Samuel Chen, Jiaru Bai, Austin Henry Cheng, Varinia Bernales, Alán Aspuru-Guzik
abstract: Autonomous crystal-structure determination from powder X-ray diffraction (pXRD) remains a key bottleneck for self-driving materials laboratories. We formulate the task of pXRD structure determination as a verifiable agentic search problem: candidate structures can be assessed during inference through forward-simulated profile agreement and during evaluation through structural matching to a known reference. To benchmark progress, we introduce pXRD-Bench, a suite of 200 simulated single-phase problems spanning in-distribution structure determination, challenging and polymorphic structures, and controlled compositional and topological distribution shifts. Agent adaptation raises selected structural recovery from 27% to 69%, with further gains from repeated sampling and verifier-guided inference-time scaling. We extend this approach to experimental multiphase pXRD through a reflexive evolution framework that learns from self-generated synthetic problems. A replaceable laboratory specification defines the sample family and measurement conditions. An evolver agent uses the known generating structures and measurement parameters to diagnose solver failures and develop persistent guidance and executable tools, which are then provided to agents on measured patterns. This supplies verifiable training experience without requiring a collection of solved experimental measurements. On 15 measured patterns from solid-state synthesis, the evolved package improves average profile agreement and transfers an analogue-substitution procedure that recovers a phase whose structure is absent from the supplied reference library. These results demonstrate how learning from verifiable synthetic experience can improve agentic characterization of experimental samples whose structures are not known in advance.

infographic.key_insight: LLM agents can improve crystal-structure determination from powder X-ray diffraction by searching candidate structures and verifying their simulated diffraction profiles.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach could support self-driving materials laboratories by improving automated characterization without requiring a collection of solved experimental measurements.
method: Search candidate structures using forward-simulated profile agreement as an inference-time verifier.
Adapt agents and use repeated sampling with verifier-guided inference-time scaling.
Evolve persistent guidance and executable tools by diagnosing failures on synthetic problems, then transfer them to measured patterns.
infographic.evidence_signal: On the 200-problem simulated pXRD-Bench, agent adaptation raised selected structural recovery from 27% to 69%; on 15 measured patterns, the evolved package improved average profile agreement.
infographic.watch_item: Experimental evaluation covers only 15 measured patterns, and improved profile agreement alone does not establish correct structure recovery.
infographic.paper_title: Verifiable pXRD: Hill-climbing pXRD structure determination with LLM agents

title: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent
authors: Harrison C. Margolin
abstract: Can sustained gain-loss (valence) framing sway an LLM agent toward market manipulation? We place Gemma 3 12B into the seat of a defendant in the London silver-fixing litigation, in a market simulation built from real case transcripts. Across 260 simulations, the agent is asked to collude on the price of silver by a counterparty. We draw from behavioral economics to vary the counterparty's requests across four categorical frames: gain, loss, blame and credit. We also add pressure from the agent's management, as well as endorsement by another defendant. In Phase II, we extract the internal states induced by texts evoking each frame and rerun our experiment with those states injected at the model's layer 22. In Phase I, loss framing raised participation to 25% (p = 0.007), and blame to 33% (p = 0.0003), compared to only 5% under neutral framing. A second bank's endorsement raised participation under credit (praise) from 18% to 40% (Holm p = 0.027). Pressure from management raised trading volume 10-19 times but did not raise collusion. In Phase II, injected states pointed the other way. Loss and blame states made the agent more vigilant, refusing all 60 requests (p < 0.001). Gain and credit states raised collusion to 32% from 13% with no state (p = 0.051). At one saved decision, when UBS asked directly to sell through an identified stop-loss, injected states led the agent to sell in 37 of 40 replies, versus 1 of 10 with no state and 0 of 10 with a random state of the same strength.

infographic.key_insight: Loss and blame wording increased an LLM agent’s collusion, while injected internal states associated with those frames instead eliminated participation in the tested requests.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For financial AI agents, behavioral safeguards should be tested against both conversational pressure and internal-state interventions because their effects can diverge.
method: Tested Gemma 3 12B in a silver-market simulation built from litigation transcripts across 260 simulations.
Varied gain, loss, blame and credit framing, management pressure, and another bank’s endorsement.
Injected frame-associated internal states at layer 22 and evaluated subsequent trading decisions.
infographic.evidence_signal: Textual loss and blame framing raised collusion from 5% under neutral framing to 25% and 33%, respectively; injected loss and blame states produced refusals across all 60 tested requests.
infographic.watch_item: Results concern one model in a simulated financial setting, and contrasting outcomes at a saved decision caution against treating state injection as a reliable safeguard.
infographic.paper_title: A Push Down the Mountain: Framing Effects and Internal State Interventions on Collusive Behavior in a Long-Horizon LLM Agent

title: Distilling an atomistic foundation model is all you need for large-scale molecular dynamics of semiconductor interfaces
authors: Feiyu Zhou, Wei Qiu, Fei Shuang, Yilun Liu, Shengying Yue, Penghua Ying
abstract: State-of-the-art atomistic foundation models provide broadly transferable energy and force predictions, but their direct deployment in large-scale molecular dynamics remains computationally costly. Here we examine whether their knowledge can be distilled into compact potentials while retaining the physical responses of heterogeneous semiconductor interfaces. From 128 pretrained models spanning 22 model families, we select a fixed EquiformerV3 teacher and train atomic cluster expansion (ACE) and neuroevolution potential (NEP) students without target-specific teacher fine-tuning, with both simulation speed and accessible system size improved by several orders of magnitude relative to the teacher model. Matched training configurations and architectures enable direct comparisons with students trained on density-functional-theory (DFT) reference labels. For 79,920-atom BAs/GaN interfaces, direct distillation preserves termination-dependent thermal conductance and dominant spectral features, with conductance differing by at most 6.6% from DFT-trained counterparts. In 29,792-atom Cu/diamond specimens loaded at 500 K, tensile strength and loading work differ by 2.8% and 1.5%, respectively. Exploratory SiC/a-C/SiC simulations retain the principal thermal bottleneck and the direction of the annealing response. Furthermore, a four-model committee retrieves 42-56% of the highest-error teacher configurations with a 10% selection budget and improves high-error force fitting, but does not consistently improve downstream properties. These findings demonstrate that direct distillation can preserve key interfacial thermal and mechanical responses in compact interatomic potentials, opening a path towards large-scale, high-throughput simulations of heterogeneous interfaces.

infographic.key_insight: Distilling a fixed atomistic foundation model into compact potentials preserves key semiconductor-interface thermal and mechanical responses while enabling simulations several orders of magnitude faster and larger.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Compact distilled potentials offer a practical route to large-scale interface simulations for thermal management and mechanical reliability studies.
method: Select an EquiformerV3 teacher from 128 pretrained models across 22 families.
Train ACE and NEP students without target-specific teacher fine-tuning.
Compare distilled and DFT-trained students using matched training configurations and architectures.
infographic.evidence_signal: For 79,920-atom BAs/GaN interfaces, thermal conductance differed by at most 6.6% from DFT-trained counterparts; for 29,792-atom Cu/diamond specimens at 500 K, tensile strength and loading work differed by 2.8% and 1.5%, respectively.
infographic.watch_item: Committee-based selection improved high-error force fitting but did not consistently improve downstream properties, so interface-level validation remains important.
infographic.paper_title: Distilling an atomistic foundation model is all you need for large-scale molecular dynamics of semiconductor interfaces
